forms of the verb to be

to be is the most important verb in the English language, an analogue of the Russian “to be/appear”. Three forms: am - only with I; is - with he, she, it; are - with you, we, they. ⚠️ An important difference from Russian: in English the verb cannot be missed.

Example: I am hungry.

Negation

Negation is constructed by adding not: am not, is not, are not. Short forms: isn't (= is not), aren't (= are not). Only am not is not reduced to amn't - an exception!

Example: I'm not a student.

Questions with to be

In questions, the verb to be is placed before the subject: She is → Is she? Special questions: question word + to be + subject: Where is he? What is this? Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't

Example: Are you a student?

Short answers

In short answers the pronoun + to be. You cannot shorten the form of the verb in an affirmative answer. Are you tired? — Yes, I am.✓ Yes, I'm. ✗

Example: Is she ready? — Yes, she is.

indefinite

a and an are the indefinite article, placed before the first mentioned object in the singular. The choice depends on the sound, not the letter: • a - before the consonant sound: a book, a car, a university [ju...] • an - before a vowel sound: an apple, an hour [aʊ...], an honest man

Example: I saw a cat in the garden.

Article the

the is used when the speaker and listener know what they are talking about. When we put the: 1. The subject has already been mentioned:I saw a cat. The cat was black. 2. One of a kind: the sun, the moon, the earth 3. It is clear from the context: Close the window, please. 4. Superlative: the best, the biggest

Example: The film we saw was amazing.

Zero article

The article is not placed before: • Proper names: John, London, Russia • Languages and nationalities: English, Russian • Sports and games: football, chess • Food/drinks in a general sense: I love coffee • Abstract concepts in general: Life is short. Love is blind. • Plural in the general sense: Dogs are friendly.

Example: She speaks Spanish.

Present Simple

Present Simple is used for: habits and regular actions, facts and general truths, schedules.

Example: I drink coffee every morning.

Present Simple

Negation is constructed using the auxiliary verb do/does + not: • I/you/we/they + don't + infinitive • he/she/it + doesn't + infinitive ⚠️ After doesn't the main verb without -s! She doesn't like (not likes).

Example: I don't eat meat.

Present Simple

Questions: Do/Does + subject + infinitive? • I/you/we/they: Do you...? • he/she/it: Does she...? Special questions: question word + do/does + subject + infinitive: Where does she live? What do they do? ⚠️ Exception: the question “Who?” without do: Who likes ice cream?

Example: Do you speak Russian?

Stative verbs

Some verbs describe a state rather than an action - they are not used in Continuous tenses. Main groups: • Opinions: know, believe, think, understand, remember, forget • Feelings: love, hate, like, want, need, prefer • Perception: see, hear, smell, taste, look • Being: be, exist, belong, contain, seem, appear

Example: I understand you.

Personal pronouns

Unlike Russian, in Englishthe subject is always obligatory. In Russian: “I’m going home.” In English: I am going home. Object forms (after a verb or preposition): me, you, him, her, it, us, them.

Example: She is a teacher.

Possessive adjectives

Possessive adjectives show ownership and go before the noun. Important: its (without apostrophe) = ownership; it's (with an apostrophe) = it is. Do not change in gender and number: my friend / my friends - the same.

Example: This is my phone.

Plural of nouns

Basic rule: add -s. Special cases: • -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: + es → boxes, watches, tomatoes • vowel + -y: + s → boys, days • consonant + -y: -y → ies → cities, babies • -f/-fe: → ves → knives, leaves, wives Irregular: child→children, man→men, woman→women, tooth→teeth, foot→feet, mouse→mice, person→people…

Example: one bus → two buses.

This / that / these / those

this (this) - singular + next these (these) - plural + nearby that (that) - singular + far or already known those (those) - plural + far Also used about time: this week (this week), that year (that year).

Example: This is my bag.

existence

The construction there is/are means “exists/exist”, “is”. • There is + singular noun. number • There are + plural noun.

Example: There is a cinema near here.

Prepositions of place

Three main prepositions: • in = inside something: in the box, in the city, in bed • on = on the surface: on the table, on the wall, on the left • at = at a specific point: at the station, at home, at school Others: under (under), next to/beside (near), behind (behind), in front of (in front), between (between)…

Example: The keys are on the table.

Imperative

Imperative = base form of a verb without a subject. Negation: Don't + infinitive Please makes the request politer (at the beginning or end). To include the speaker: Let's + infinitive → Let's go! Let's eat!

Example: Turn left at the crossroads.

skill and resolution

can is a modal verb, expresses: 1. Skill/Ability: I can play the guitar 2. Opportunity: It can be dangerous 3. Resolution (spoken): Can I use your phone? ⚠️ can never changes: he can (not he cans). After it there is an infinitive without to.

Example: I can speak three languages.

Question words

Question words appear at the beginning of the question, followed by an auxiliary verb before the subject.

Example: Where does she work?

Quantitative numerals

Numerals 1–12: special words (one, two, three... twelve). 13–19: + -teen (thirteen, fourteen... nineteen; exceptions: thirteen, fifteen, eighteen). Tens: twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety. Compounds: 21 = twenty-one (via hyphen). 100 = a/one hundred; 1000 = a/one thousand.

Example: She is twenty-three years old.

Ordinal numbers

Ordinal numbers are formed by adding -th: fourth, fifth, sixth... Exceptions: first (1st), second (2nd), third (3rd), fifth (5th), eighth (8th), ninth (9th), twelfth (12th). Always used with the article the: the first day, the third floor. Fractions: ½ = a half, ⅓ = a third, ¼ = a quarter.

Example: My office is on the third floor.

Possessive case

In English, belonging is expressed by an apostrophe + s: • Singular: Tom's book, the dog's tail • Plural with -s: apostrophe only: the teachers' room, my parents' house • Irregular plural: 's: the children's playground, men's clothes • Names ending with -s: James's / James' - both options are correct

Example: This is Anna's laptop.

Prepositions of movement

• to = direction to a point: go to work, walk to the park • into = movement inward: come into the room, jump into the pool • out of = movement outward: get out of the car, take out of the bag • up/down = up/down: climb up the hill, walk down the stairs • along = along: walk along the river • across = across/through…

Example: She walked into the room.

Past Simple

Past Simple - a completed action in the past with or without a specific tense. Rules for writing the ending -ed: • Most verbs: + ed → worked, played • End in -e: + d → loved, used • Consonant + -y: -y → ied → studied, tried • One vowel + one consonant (short stressed syllable): double the consonant → stopped, planned

Example: She worked all day yesterday.

Past Simple

About 200 irregular verbs need to be learned by heart. The most frequent 50 cover ~90% of uses. Groups by similarity of changes: • AAA (do not change): cut, put, hit, set, let • ABA (return to the beginning): run→ran→run, come→came→come • ABC (all different): go→went→gone, be→was/were→been

Example: I went to Paris last summer.

Past Simple

Negation: didn't (= did not) + infinitive for all persons. ⚠️ After didn't - base form of the verb (not past tense!): She didn't go (not went).

Example: I didn't see him yesterday.

Past Simple

Question: Did + subject + infinitive? Special questions: Where/When/What + did + subject + infinitive? ⚠️ Exception: the question “Who performed the action?” is built without did: Who called? Who broke the vase?

Example: Did you enjoy the film?

verb to be in the past

Past tense of the verb to be: • was - with I, he, she, it • were - with you, we, they Negation: wasn't / weren't Question: Was she...? Were they...?

Example: I was very tired last night.

predictions and spontaneous decisions

will is used for: 1. Spontaneous decisions (made at the time of speech): I'll help you with that. 2. Predictions without a specific plan: I think it will rain. 3. Promises: I won't tell anyone. 4. Requests: Will you open the window? Abbreviation: 'll. Negation: won't (= will not).

Example: The phone is ringing. — I'll get it!

intentions and obvious predictions

going to is used for: 1. Pre-made decisions and intentions: I'm going to start a diet next week. 2. Predictions with visible signs: Look at those clouds - it's going to rain! Form: am/is/are + going to + infinitive

Example: I'm going to study medicine.

Present Continuous

Present Continuous is an action taking place right now or temporarily during this period. Form: am/is/are + verb + -ing Rules for writing -ing: • Most: just + ing → working, playing • Ends with -e: remove -e + ing → making, coming • Short stressed syllable: double the last consonant → running, sitting

Example: I am studying English right now.

Present Continuous for planned future

Present Continuous is used for specific agreements in the future - when the time and place have already been determined. Difference: • I'm meeting Alice tomorrow - the meeting has been agreed (a specific plan) • I'll meet Alice tomorrow - intention or proposal

Example: I'm having dinner with Alex tonight.

Present Simple vs Present Continuous

Present Simple: habits, facts, schedules, general truths. Present Continuous: something that is happening right now or temporarily. Compare: • She speaks French. - knows the language (always) • She is speaking French. - speaks right now ⚠️ Stative verbs (know, love, want, understand...) - only Present Simple!

Example: Water boils at 100°C.

advice and recommendation

should expresses mild advice or personal opinion. Weaker than must. After should - infinitive without to. Also used for criticism or regret: You should have called (should have called).

Example: You should exercise more.

obligation and strict prohibition

must - a strong obligation (often internal) or a categorical requirement. mustn't - a strict prohibition (absolutely impossible!). ⚠️ Important difference: mustn't ≠ don't have to! • mustn't = prohibited • don't have to = not required, but possible

Example: You must show your passport.

external necessity

have to - a necessity due to external rules, circumstances or other people's requirements. Difference from must: • must - internal necessity: I must call her (I myself consider it necessary) • have to - external: I have to wear a uniform (rule) don't have to=optional (not necessary, but allowed).

Example: I have to finish this report by Friday.

past skill and polite requests

could is the past tense of can. Two main meanings: 1. Skill in the past: I could read at 4 years old. 2. Polite requests (more polite than can): Could you pass the salt, please? Also for present possibility: It could be true.

Example: She could play the violin as a child.

Comparative degree of adjectives

Monosyllabic and disyllabic in -y: + er (fast→faster, happy→happier). Polysyllabic: more + adjective. Writing rules: -e → + r (nice→nicer); short stressed syllable: double (big→bigger); -y → ier (heavy→heavier).

Example: This film is more interesting than that one.

Superlative adjectives

Monosyllabic: the + -est. Polysyllabic: the most. The writing rules are the same as for the comparative degree. Irregular: good→the best, bad→the worst, far→the furthest, much/many→the most ⚠️ Always with the article the! After superlatives, often in or of: the tallest girl in the class.

Example: This is the most expensive restaurant in the city.

indefinite amount

some - in affirmative sentences and in offers/requests. any - in questions and negations. Exception: some in questions when we expect an affirmative answer or offer something: Would you like some tea? Can I have some water?

Example: I bought some bread and some milk.

much / many / a lot of / a few / a little

much - with uncountables (much water, much time, much money). many - with countables (many people, many books, many times). a lot of / lots of - with both, conversational style. a few - a little (countable, neutral/positive). few - few, almost none (countable, negative). a little - a little (uncountable, neutral).

Example: I don't have much time.

Countable and uncountable nouns

Countable: you can count, there are plural. number: a book, two books. Uncountable: cannot be counted directly - no plural. numbers, no indefinite article.

Example: Can I have some information, please?

Prepositions in / on / at for time

at → exact time: at 6 o'clock, at noon, at midnight, at night, at the weekend (BrE) on → days and dates: on Monday, on 5 March, on my birthday, on New Year's Day in → periods: in July, in 2023, in the morning/afternoon/evening, in summer, in the 21st century Without preposition: this/last/next + time: this morning…

Example: The meeting is at half past three.

duration and beginning

for - duration (how long): for two hours, for a week, for years. Used with different tenses. since - initial moment (since): since Monday, since 2019, since I was a child. Used with the Present Perfect. ago - time ago from now: three days ago, a month ago. Only with Past Simple.

Example: I've been here for six months.

Tail questions

Tag questions are used to confirm or clarify. Rule: affirmative sentence → negative tag, and vice versa. Auxiliary verb in the tail = tense of the main sentence. Intonation: ↘ (falling) = confirmation; ↗ (rising) = real question.

Example: It's a nice day, isn't it?

possession (British version)

have got is a colloquial British form of possession. Value = have. • Affirmation: I have got / I've got a laptop. • Denial: I haven't got / I don't have • Question: Have you got...? / Do you have...? ⚠️ have got is used only in the present. For the past - only had.

Example: I've got two brothers.

Adverbs of manner

Most adverbs are formed from adjectives + -ly: quick → quickly, careful → carefully, slow → slowly.

Example: He explained it clearly.

Adverbs of frequency and their place in a sentence

Adverbs of frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, occasionally, rarely, rarely, never. Place in a sentence: • Before the main verb: She always drinks tea. • After the verb to be: He is always late. • After the auxiliary verb: She has never been to Italy.

Example: I usually wake up at 7.

Order of adjectives before nouns

When several adjectives appear before a noun, a strict order is observed: Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose (Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose) Example: a small beautiful old square brown French wooden writing desk

Example: a lovely little old cottage.

Present Perfect

Present Perfect = have/has + V3 (third form of the verb). Three main meanings: 1. Life Experience (no time specified): I have visited Tokyo. 2. Result in the present: I have lost my keys. (there are no keys now) 3. Unfinished action, ongoing now: She has lived here for 5 years.

Example: Have you ever eaten sushi?

Present Perfect markers

ever - someday (in questions about experience). Location: in front of V3. never - never (negative value). Location: in front of V3. already - already (earlier than expected). Place: before V3 or at the end. yet - already/yet. In questions (Have you finished yet?) and negations (I haven't finished yet).

Example: Have you ever been to Scotland?

Present Perfect vs Past Simple

This is one of the most important differences in English grammar. Present Perfect - connection with the present, time is NOT indicated: I've lost my wallet. (no wallet now - this is important) Past Simple - completed past, time is indicated or implied: I lost my wallet yesterday.

Example: I've met the new director.

Present Perfect with for and since

for - duration: for two days, for a year, for a long time, for ages since - starting point: since Monday, since I was a child, since 2015 The question “How long?” — How long + Present Perfect: How long have you known her?

Example: She's worked here for ten years.

Present Perfect Continuous

Present Perfect Continuous = have/has been + V-ing Emphasis on duration or incompleteness of action. Answers the question “How long?” Often explains the visible result in the present: You look tired - have you been running? Difference with Present Perfect Simple: • I've read 50 pages.

Example: I've been learning English for two years.

Past Continuous

Past Continuous = was/were + V-ing Values: 1. Action in process at a specific moment in the past: At 9pm I was having dinner. 2. Background activity interrupted by another: I was walking when it started to rain. 3. Parallel actions: While she was cooking, he was watching TV.

Example: It was raining when I left home.

Past Simple vs Past Continuous

Typical design: long background action (Past Continuous) + short event (Past Simple). Unions: • when - used with the Past Simple for the event: She was sleeping when the alarm went off. • while/as - used with Past Continuous for background: While I was watching TV, the power went out.

Example: She was having a bath when the phone rang.

Type 0

Type zero - for scientific facts, laws of nature, general truths. Both actions always happen together. Form: If + Present Simple, Present Simple Instead of if you can use when: When you mix red and blue, you get purple.

Example: If you heat ice, it melts.

1st type

A real, probable situation in the future. Form: If + Present Simple, will + infinitive ⚠️ In the if-part - NEVER Future! Only Present Simple. Instead of will in the main part you can: can, may, might, should. Parts can be changed: I'll stay home if it rains. (without comma)

Example: If she studies hard, she'll pass the exam.

Type 2

An unreal or unlikely situation in the present or future. Form: If + Past Simple, would + infinitive ⚠️ The verb in the if-part is Past Simple, but the meaning is present/future! ⚠️ were is used for all persons: If I were you, If she were here is a formal language standard.

Example: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.

Type 1 vs Type 2: real vs unlikely

The choice of type reflectsyour confidencein the reality of the situation. • If I see her (1st type) - I expect to see her • If I saw her (2nd type) - unlikely or I’m just fantasizing This is not a difference in grammar, but a difference in the attitude of the speaker.

Example: If it rains tomorrow, I'll take an umbrella.

Passive Voice

Passive voice is used when: • The action itself is important, not the person who performs it • Performer unknown or obvious Form Present Simple Passive: am/is/are + V3 The performer (if needed) is added with by: The window was broken by the ball.

Example: English is spoken in many countries.

Passive Voice

Past Simple Passive: was/were + V3 • was - units. number • were - plural. number Active → Passive: Someone stole my car. → My car was stolen.

Example: The Eiffel Tower was built in 1889.

Passive Voice

Present Perfect Passive: has/have been + V3 Used when the result in the present is important, and not when exactly it happened.

Example: The project has been completed.

Reported Speech

When translated into indirect speech, the tenses are “shifted” back: • Present Simple → Past Simple: "I work" → he said he worked • Past Simple → Past Perfect: "I went" → she said she had gone • Present Perfect → Past Perfect: "I've seen" → he said he had seen • will → would; can → could; is → was; am going → was going

Example: She said: 'I am leaving.' → She said she was leaving.

Reported questions

In indirect questions: 1. No inversion (word order as in the statement) 2. No auxiliary do/did 3. General questions (Yes/No) → if/whether + subject + verb

Example: Where do you work?" → She asked where I worked.

say vs tell in indirect speech

say - without the required addition: She said she was tired. tell - ALWAYS with an addition (to whom it is told): She told me she was tired. ❌ He told that he was late. ✓ He said that he was late.

Example: She said she needed help.

Verbs + gerund (V-ing)

These verbs require a gerund (V-ing) after them: enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, suggest, keep, consider, deny, imagine, miss, practice, risk, admit, delay, dislike, fancy, give up, involve, put off, recommend, resist Memorization trick: if you can replace it with “process”, it’s most likely a gerund.

Example: I enjoy swimming in the sea.

Verbs + infinitive (to + V)

These verbs require an infinitive with to: want, decide, hope, plan, manage, agree, promise, refuse, fail, expect, offer, learn, need, afford, arrange, attempt, choose, claim, demand, deserve, help, pretend, tend, threaten

Example: She decided to quit her job.

Verbs with both (like, love, hate, start, begin)

After like/love/hate/prefer both options are possible: • V-ing - we talk about the action as a whole: I love cooking. (I generally like to cook) • to-inf - we are talking about a specific case: I'd like to cook tonight. After start/begin/continue/cease there is practically no difference.

Example: I love travelling / to travel.

past habits and states

used to - regular actions or conditions in the past that have already stopped. Form: used to + infinitive Denial: didn't use to Question: Did you use to...? ⚠️ There is no present tense form! You can't: I use to for the present. Difference from be used to: I am used to waking up early = I'm used to it (now).

Example: I used to smoke, but I stopped.

Relative clauses

who - for people: The woman who called is my sister. which - for objects and animals: The book which I borrowed was great. that - for people and objects (in defining clauses): The car that he bought is new. where - for places: The café where we met is closed. whose - accessory: The girl whose bag was stolen...

Example: The man who lives next door is very friendly.

Conjunctions of contrast

although / even though / though + subordinate clause. despite / in spite of + noun / gerund (NOT subordinate clause!). however + new sentence (after period or semicolon). whereas is a contrast between two facts.

Example: Although she was tired, she kept working.

Future Continuous

Future Continuous = will be + V-ing Values: 1. An action that will be in progress at a specific moment in the future: At this time tomorrow, I'll be lying on the beach. 2. Planned, expected action in the future (natural course of events): I'll be seeing her tomorrow anyway. 3.

Example: Don't call at 8 — I'll be having dinner.

Future Perfect

Future Perfect = will have + V3 An action that will be completed before a certain point in the future. Often used with by (the time), before: By the time you arrive, I will have cooked dinner.

Example: I'll have finished this book by Sunday.

Subordinate goals

to / in order to / so as to + infinitive - goal. In order to and so as to are a little more formal. so that + subject + verb - purpose with another subject or with a modal. ⚠️ Denial: in order not to / so as not to (not to not).

Example: She studies hard in order to get a scholarship.

Phrasal verbs

Phrasal verbs = verb + particle (preposition or adverb). The meaning is often idiomatic.

Example: I've given up smoking.

Past Perfect Simple

Past Perfect - an action that completed before another moment or event in the past. Form: had + V3 for all faces. Negation: hadn't + V3 Question: Had + subject + V3? Typical conjunctions: before, after, when, by the time, already, just, never

Example: When I arrived, she had already left.

Past Perfect Continuous

Past Perfect Continuous = had been + V-ing Emphasis on the duration of an action that occurred before another point in the past. Often explains a cause or visible result in the past.

Example: She was exhausted — she'd been working all night.

confident conclusion about the past

must have + V3 = I'm sure this happened (the only logical explanation). Confidence scale: • must have done - almost certainly happened • should have done - it was expected to happen • may/might have done - it may have happened • can't have done - it probably didn't happen

Example: You must have been exhausted after that journey.

impossibility in the past

can't have + V3 = I'm sure this didn't happen (it's impossible). The opposite of must have done.

Example: He can't have seen her — she was abroad.

reproach and regret

should have + V3 = it would have been right to do it, but I didn’t (regret, reproach). shouldn't have + V3 = shouldn't have done. This is a very common construction for expressing regret and criticism.

Example: I should have brought an umbrella.

possibility in the past

might/could have + V3 = this may have happened (we don't know for sure). Also: could have done = could have done (but didn’t): I could have won if I had tried harder.

Example: She might have forgotten about the meeting.

3rd type of conditional

An unreal situation in the past - we are talking about something that did not happen. Form: If + Past Perfect, would have + V3 Both elements are unreal: • Condition not met • There was no result either

Example: If she had taken the medicine, she would have recovered.

Mixed conditionals

Mixed conditionals connect different time plans: 1. Past condition → present result: If + Past Perfect, would + infinitive If I had taken that job, I would be in New York now. 2. Present condition → past result: If + Past Simple, would have + V3 If she were more careful, she wouldn't have broken it.

Example: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

Future Passive and Passive with modals

Modal + Passive: modal + be + V3 • will be done - will be done • must be done - must be done • should be done - should be done • can be done - can be done

Example: The report will be published tomorrow.

I had my hair cut. She got her car fixed.

have/get + object + V3 - you order a service or someone does something for you. Compare: • I cut my hair. - I cut my hair myself (which is not typical) • I had my hair cut. - cut by a hairdresser get is a little more conversational, have is a little more formal.

Example: I need to have my teeth checked.

Passive reporting verbs

Two construction options with the verbs say, think, believe, report, know, expect, consider: 1. It + passive + that + subordinate clause: It is believed that... 2. Subject + is + V3 + to-infinitive: She is believed to be... Used in news and official texts.

Example: It is reported that three people were injured.

difference in meaning

remember/forget + V-ing - about a past event that we remember/forgot. remember/forget + to-inf - about the task: remember to do something in the future.

Example: I remember meeting her at a conference.

She stopped smoking vs She stopped to smoke

stop + V-ing - stop the action. stop + to-inf - stop to do something else. regret + V-ing - to regret the past. regret + to-inf - regret to inform you (formally): I regret to inform you... mean + V-ing - mean: This means working harder. mean + to-inf - intend: I meant to call you.

Example: He stopped smoking last year.

desire to change the present

wish + Past Simple - about an unrealistic desire in the present. The form is the same as in the 2nd type of conditional. For to be - were (formally), although was is also used.

Example: I wish I spoke better English.

regret about the past

wish + Past Perfect - regret about past events that cannot be changed. The form is as in the 3rd type of conditional.

Example: I wish I hadn't eaten so much.

desire to change someone else's behavior

wish + would - irritation due to someone else's behavior or a desire to change the situation. ⚠️ You cannot use about yourself: I wish I would - only about other persons or the weather/situation.

Example: I wish you would listen to me.

Defining vs non-defining clauses

Defining (defining): without commas - they clarify who/what they are talking about. The pronoun can be replaced with that. It cannot be removed without losing the meaning. Non-defining: with commas - add information without changing the meaning. That cannot be used. Can be removed.

Example: The film that I told you about is on tonight.

Prepositions in relative clauses

In colloquial speech, the preposition comes at the end: the house I grew up in. In written/formal speech, the preposition before which/whom: the house in which I grew up. After the preposition - only which (for things) and whom (for people). Never that!

Example: The project I'm working on is fascinating.

Consequence conjunctions

so + adjective/adverb + that: He spoke so quickly that nobody understood. such + (a/an) + adjective + noun + that: It was such a long film that I fell asleep. Connecting words of result (between sentences): therefore, consequently, as a result, hence, thus.

Example: It was such a good book that I read it twice.

habit (real)

be used to + V-ing / noun = to be used to (already used to). get used to + V-ing / noun = get used to (the process of getting used to). ⚠️ Not to be confused with used to + infinitive (past habits). • I used to live in Paris. - used to live (no longer) • I am used to living in big cities. - used to living in big cities

Example: I'm not used to getting up so early.

Future in the Past

Future in the Past - constructions that express the future from the point of view of the past. Used in indirect speech and narrative. • would + V (from will): She said she would come. • was/were going to + V: He was going to call but forgot. • was about to + V: She was about to leave when he arrived.

Example: She promised she would be there.

official appointment and order

be to + infinitive - official orders, planned events and fate in the narrative. 1. Legal Instruction: Passengers are to remain seated. 2. Official plan: The summit is to take place next month. 3. Fate in the narrative: They were never to meet again.

Example: You are to submit the report by Friday.

moral duty and logical expectation

ought to is a moral obligation or logical expectation. Stronger should. Always with to: ought to go (as opposed to should). For the past: ought to have + V3 - reproach or regret.

Example: You ought to apologise for what you said.

modal and regular verb

need as a modal (formal, in questions/negations) and as a regular verb. Modal (without -s, without to): • You needn't worry. / Need I explain? Regular need + to: • She doesn't need to come.

Example: You needn't fill in both forms.

courage and challenge

dare - dare, dare. Modal in rhetorical questions and negations. Modal: How dare you! / I daren't ask. / Dare I say... Normal: She didn't dare to look. / He dared to challenge the boss. ⚠️ I dare say = perhaps, probably (stable expression).

Example: How dare you speak to me like that!

Reflexive pronouns

myself, yourself, yourself, yourself, yourself, yourself, yourselves, yourself. 1. The action is directed towards the subject: He cut himself. 2. Emphase (by yourself, without help): I did it myself. Stable: by myself = alone; help yourself = help yourself.

Example: She taught herself to play the guitar.

Collective nouns

Collective nouns are a group as a whole. • BrE: usually plural. number: The team are playing. • AmE: usually units. number: The team is playing. Frequent: team, family, government, committee, staff, audience, crew, police, army, public, management

Example: The government have announced new measures. (BrE).

Fractions and mathematics

Fractions:½ = a half; ⅓ = a third; ¼ = a quarter; ¾ = three quarters; ⅔ = two thirds. Numerator is quantitative, denominator is ordinal (plural if numerator > 1). Decimals: period (not comma): 3.14 = three point one four. Mathematics: + = plus; - = minus; × = times; ÷ = divided by; = = equals.

Example: Three quarters of students passed the exam.

Degrees of comparison of adverbs

Adverbs form degrees of comparison according to the same rules as adjectives. • Monosyllabic: + er/est: fast→faster, hard→harder, early→earlier • Most on -ly: more/most: carefully→more carefully→most carefully • Incorrect: well→better→best, badly→worse→worst, far→further→furthest, little→less→least, much→more→most

Example: She spoke more confidently than before.

Inversion with negative adverbs

For emphasis, the negative adverb/expression is placed at the beginning → auxiliary verb before the subject (word order as in a question). Words that trigger inversion: never, rarely, rarely, little, hardly, scarcely, barely, not only, only, no sooner

Example: Never have I seen anything so beautiful.

Not only... but also with inversion

Not only + inversion in the first part, the second part is the usual order. Used for emphasis: expresses that something went further than expected.

Example: Not only is she talented, but she is also very hard-working.

Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.

Immediate sequence constructions: • Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when/before + Past Simple • No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than + Past Simple

Example: Hardly had she arrived when it started to rain.

Inversion in conditionals

Formal style - excludes if, uses inversion: • Had + subject + V3 = If + Past Perfect (3rd type) • Were + subject (+ to + infinitive) = If + Past Simple (2nd type) • Should + subject + infinitive = If (unlikely, type 1)

Example: Had she told me, I would have helped.

It-cleft: It was John who called.

Structure: It + to be + selected element + who/that/which + rest Shifts the focus of attention to the highlighted element. • For people - who; for things/circumstances - that/which.

Example: It was the noise that woke me up.

Wh-cleft: What surprised me was the price.

Structure: What + subordinate clause + to be + highlighted element Emphasizes the importance of the element introduced at the end.

Example: What I love about London is the diversity.

Formal subjunctive after verbs of demand

After suggest, recommend, insist, demand, propose, request, require, ask, advise, order + that - the basic form of the verb for all persons (without -s, without was). The British version often uses should instead of the subjunctive: I suggest that he should leave. American - often a pure subjunctive.

Example: I recommend that he see a doctor.

It's high time + Past Simple

It's (high/about) time + subject + Past Simple Meaning: present/future - we are talking about something that should have been done a long time ago. high time - even stronger: it’s high time!

Example: It's time she found a new job.

as if / as though + subjunctive

as if / as though + Past Simple is an unrealistic comparison in the present. as if / as though + Past Perfect is an unrealistic comparison about the past.

Example: He spends money as if he were a millionaire.

So do I. Neither does she. So am I.

So + auxiliary + subject - agreement with the affirmative. Neither/Nor + auxiliary + subject - agreement with the negative. The auxiliary verb must coincide with the tense of the original sentence.

Example: I love jazz. So does she.

I think so / I hope so / I'm afraid so

so replaces the subordinate clause after: think, hope, suppose, expect, believe, imagine, be afraid. Negative form: not (not so not!).

Example: Will he come? — I think so. / I don't think so.

Inclusive vs non-inclusive clauses

Defining: specifies who/what we are talking about - without commas. that is possible. The pronoun can be omitted if it is an object. Non-defining: adds information - commas required. Only who/which (not that!). The pronoun cannot be omitted.

Example: The film that won the Oscar was brilliant.

Preposition + which/whom in formal style

Formal style: preposition + which/whom before a relative pronoun. Informal equivalent: preposition at the end of a sentence. whom is the formal object form of who.

Example: The report to which I referred is attached.

Nominalization

Nominalization is the conversion of verbs/adjectives into nouns. A sign of academic and business style.

Example: She decided to expand. → Our decision to expand the company...

Nominalization in academic text

Nominalization allows: 1. Compress information: There was a significant increase in prices. 2. Add definitions: The rapid increase in house prices... 3. Create a formal, impersonal tone.

Example: There has been a significant improvement in air quality.

Present participle: V-ing clause

The participial phrase with Present Participle (V-ing) replaces the subordinate clause: • Simultaneity: Walking home, I noticed something strange. (= While I was walking home) • Reason: Knowing the answer, she raised her hand.

Example: Arriving at the airport, he realised he had forgotten his passport.

Past participial phrase

V3 clause (Past Participle) = passive meaning: Built in 1889, the Eiffel Tower... Having + V3 = action completed before the main one: Having read the report, he called a meeting. (= After he had read...)

Example: Surprised by the news, she sat down silently.

Conditional with unless / provided / as long as / on…

unless = if not (but cannot be used with negation!): Unless you hurry = If you don't hurry provided/providing (that) = if and only if (strict condition) as long as = provided that (assumption) on condition that = on condition that (formally) in case = in case

Example: I'll lend you money, as long as you pay me back.

Suppose you won the lottery

Suppose/Supposing - used as if in hypothetical questions. What if is an informal analogue. With Past Simple - a situation is unlikely or imaginary.

Example: Supposing you had to choose — which would you pick?

Only + circumstance + inversion

Only + when/after/if/then/by/in/on - the entire group is moved to the beginning → inversion. This is one of the most powerful rhetorical devices in writing and public speaking.

Example: Only when you experience it can you truly understand.

So + adjective/adverb + inversion

Book and oratorical style. So + adj/adv + be/aux + subject Such + was/were + subject

Example: So rapid was the change that nobody could adapt.

Hedging

Hedging is the deliberate softening of statements to express scientific modesty. Main structures: • appear/seem to - apparently • tend to - as a rule, tend to • be likely/unlikely to - likely/unlikely • be thought/considered to be - it is believed that

Example: The results appear to suggest a correlation.

Discourse markers in academic text

Markers structure and connect academic text: • Addition: Moreover, Furthermore, In addition, Additionally • Contrast: However, nevertheless, nevertheless, Conversely, On the other hand • Result: Therefore, Consequently, As a result, Hence, Thus • Explanation: In other words, That is to say, Namely • Concession…

Example: The experiment failed. Nevertheless, the findings were instructive.

Speech registers

Register is determined by purpose, audience and context. Formal: passive, nominalization, complex conjunctions, full forms, verbs of Latin origin (commence, terminate, assist). Neutral: standard grammar, no slang, moderate abbreviations.

Example: Formal: I wish to draw your attention to a discrepancy.

Connotations of synonyms

Synonyms differ in connotation (emotional coloring) and register. Examples of scales: • slim (+) → thin (0) → skinny (-) → scrawny/gaunt (--) • determined (+) → firm (0) → stubborn/pig-headed (-) • thrifty (+) → economical (0) → stingy/tight-fisted (-) • confident (+) → assertive (0) → arrogant (-)

Example: She is slim. (+) / She is thin. (0) / She is skinny. (-).

Rhetorical devices

Anaphora: repetition of words at the beginning of successive sentences. "I have a dream... I have a dream..." Chiasmus: AB-BA cross structure. "Ask not what your country can do for you, but what you can do for your country." Tricolon: three parallel elements.

Example: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.

Precise collocations in academic text

In C2 it is important to use the 'correct' verb with each noun. Academic collocations: • conduct/carry out research (not make/do) • draw/reach a conclusion • raise/address/tackle an issue • reach/achieve a consensus • make significant progress • pose/present a challenge

Example: Researchers conducted extensive interviews.

Absolute construction with participle

Absolute construction = noun/pronoun + participle (independent subject). Used in written and formal style - adds a circumstance without a conjunction.

Example: All things considered, it was a successful event.

Ellipsis and substitution in connected text

Ellipsis is the omission of already known elements. Substitution - using do/so/one/it instead of repeating. Ellipse types: • A: Are you coming? B: Might (do). • She speaks French and he does too / so does he. • I wanted to leave, but wasn't allowed to. (leave omitted) Substitution: I thought he'd pass. He did.

Example: Can you drive? — I used to (drive).

Infinitive phrases instead of subordinate clauses

Complex infinitive (Complex Object) replaces the subordinate clause: I want + object + to-infinitive: I want her to stay. After see, hear, watch, let, make, have - infinitive without to: I saw her leave. / She made him cry. / Let me help. In the passive - with to: He was made to pay.

Example: I need you to sign this document.

Future Perfect Continuous

Future Perfect Continuous = will have been + V-ing Emphasis on the duration of an action that will last until a certain point in the future. Often answers the question “How long by then?” Often used with by (the time), for, when: By Monday, she will have been working on this project for three weeks.

Example: By next year, I will have been learning English for five years.

Coordination of tenses

In complex sentences, the verb of the subordinate clause agrees in time with the main one.

Example: He told me that he had been living there for years.

Coordinating conjunctions

Coordinating conjunctions connect equivalent parts of a sentence. Seven Basic (acronym FANBOYS): • for = because (formal): She left, for she was tired. • and = and (adding) • nor = and not (Neither/Nor... inversion!): She didn't call, nor did she write.

Example: She was tired, yet she kept working.

Subordinating conjunctions

Subordinating conjunctions introduce subordinate clauses. By value: • Time: when, while, as, after, before, until, once, as soon as, whenever • Reasons: because, since, as, given that, seeing that • Conditions: if, unless, provided, as long as, in case, supposing • Goals: so that, in order that, best • Concessions…

Example: Seeing that the deadline had passed, we cancelled the meeting.

Comma, semicolon and colon

Comma: • Before coordinating conjunctions FANBOYS between independent clauses. • After introductory words/turns of phrase: However, she decided to stay. • In the enumerations (Oxford comma - before the last and): apples, oranges, and bananas. Semicolon (;): connects two independent clauses without a conjunction.

Example: However, the results were inconclusive; further research is required.

Dash, apostrophe and quotation marks

Dash (—): highlights a plug-in construction (stronger than a comma): The solution - though expensive - proven effective.

Example: The project — launched in 2020 — exceeded all expectations.

Special and indirect questions in academic text

In academic texts, direct questions are replaced by indirect ones (interrogative clauses). An indirect question is a subordinate clause with the usual word order (without inversion, without do). Introductory words: whether, if (yes/no), what, where, when, how, why, which.

Example: I wonder whether the hypothesis is correct.

Preposition (A2)

Use 'interested in' before a noun or gerund. Wrong: “I am interested on improving my speaking.” → Right: “I am interested in improving my speaking.”.

Example: I am interested in improving my speaking.

Article (A2)

Use an article before singular countable nouns like 'meeting'. Wrong: “I had meeting with manager yesterday.” → Right: “I had a meeting with my manager yesterday.”.

Example: I had a meeting with my manager yesterday.

Word Order (A2)

In standard word order, the object usually comes before 'very much'. Wrong: “I like very much this course.” → Right: “I like this course very much.”.

Example: I like this course very much.

Tense (B1)

Use the present perfect with 'for' to describe a duration that started in the past and continues now. Wrong: “I work here since two years.” → Right: “I have worked here for two years.”.

Example: I have worked here for two years.

Countability (B1)

'Advice' is uncountable in English, so do not use 'an' before it. Wrong: “I need an advice about my interview.” → Right: “I need some advice about my interview.”.

Example: I need some advice about my interview.

Verb Pattern (B1)

After 'enjoy', use a gerund: enjoy doing something. Wrong: “I enjoy to speak with new people.” → Right: “I enjoy speaking with new people.”.

Example: I enjoy speaking with new people.

Question (A2)

Use auxiliary 'do' in present simple information questions. Wrong: “Where you live now?” → Right: “Where do you live now?”.

Example: Where do you live now?

Preposition (B1)

Use 'arrive at' for specific places like airports, stations, and buildings. Wrong: “I arrived to the airport at 7.” → Right: “I arrived at the airport at 7.”.

Example: I arrived at the airport at 7.

Word Choice (B1)

Use 'take an exam' for doing the exam. Use 'pass an exam' only when the result is successful. Wrong: “I passed an exam last Friday.” → Right: “I took an exam last Friday.”.

Example: I took an exam last Friday.

Collocation (B1)

'Pronunciation mistake' is a more natural collocation than 'mistake in the pronunciation'. Wrong: “I made a mistake in the pronunciation.” → Right: “I made a pronunciation mistake.”.

Example: I made a pronunciation mistake.

Tense (B1)

Stative verbs like 'know' usually use simple tenses, not continuous tenses. Wrong: “I was knowing the answer, but I forgot it.” → Right: “I knew the answer, but I forgot it.”.

Example: I knew the answer, but I forgot it.

Modal (B1)

After modal verbs like 'must', use the base verb without 'to'. Wrong: “You must to practice every day.” → Right: “You must practice every day.”.

Example: You must practice every day.

Preposition (B1)

The standard phrase is 'depend on'. Wrong: “It depends from the situation.” → Right: “It depends on the situation.”.

Example: It depends on the situation.

Word Choice (A2)

Use 'to' plus the base verb to explain purpose. Wrong: “I am learning English for find a better job.” → Right: “I am learning English to find a better job.”.

Example: I am learning English to find a better job.

Article (A2)

Use 'the' before superlatives like 'best'. Wrong: “She is best developer in our team.” → Right: “She is the best developer on our team.”.

Example: She is the best developer on our team.

Conditional (B1)

In first conditional sentences, use present simple after 'if'. Wrong: “If I will have time, I will join the call.” → Right: “If I have time, I will join the call.”.

Example: If I have time, I will join the call.

Pronoun (A2)

Use subject pronouns before the verb. In formal English, put the other person first. Wrong: “Me and my friend watched a movie.” → Right: “My friend and I watched a movie.”.

Example: My friend and I watched a movie.

Countability (B1)

'Homework' is uncountable, so it does not usually take a plural form. Wrong: “I have many homeworks this week.” → Right: “I have a lot of homework this week.”.

Example: I have a lot of homework this week.

Verb Pattern (B2)

In standard English, 'suggest' is not followed by object plus infinitive. Use 'suggest that...' or 'suggest doing...'. Wrong: “I suggested him to try another approach.” → Right: “I suggested that he try another approach.”.

Example: I suggested that he try another approach.

Word Order (B1)

Move 'only' near the phrase it limits and use 'for' with a duration. Wrong: “I only worked there three months.” → Right: “I worked there for only three months.”.

Example: I worked there for only three months.

Collocation (B2)

Use 'make a decision', not 'do a decision'. Wrong: “I did a decision after the interview.” → Right: “I made a decision after the interview.”.

Example: I made a decision after the interview.

Question (B1)

In embedded questions, use statement word order after the question phrase. Wrong: “Can you tell me where is the meeting room?” → Right: “Can you tell me where the meeting room is?”.

Example: Can you tell me where the meeting room is?

Tense (B2)

Use past simple for finished past habits with a finished time reference. Wrong: “When I was a child, I have played football every day.” → Right: “When I was a child, I played football every day.”.

Example: When I was a child, I played football every day.

Word Choice (B1)

'Agree' is a verb, so do not use 'am' before it. Wrong: “I am agree with your opinion.” → Right: “I agree with your opinion.”.

Example: I agree with your opinion.

Preposition (B1)

Use 'good at' before a noun or gerund. Wrong: “I am good in explaining technical things.” → Right: “I am good at explaining technical things.”.

Example: I am good at explaining technical things.

Modal (B2)

After 'should have', use the past participle form of the main verb. Wrong: “I should have went earlier.” → Right: “I should have gone earlier.”.

Example: I should have gone earlier.

Conditional (B2)

Use past perfect in the if-clause and 'would have' plus past participle for third conditional. Wrong: “If I knew about the problem, I would fixed it.” → Right: “If I had known about the problem, I would have fixed it.”.

Example: If I had known about the problem, I would have fixed it.

Article (B1)

Use 'the office' when referring to a known workplace. Wrong: “I went to office after lunch.” → Right: “I went to the office after lunch.”.

Example: I went to the office after lunch.

Word Choice (B2)

Use 'currently' for 'at the moment'. 'Actually' usually means 'in fact'. Wrong: “Actually I work as a QA engineer since 2022.” → Right: “Currently, I work as a QA engineer, and I have been in this role since 2022.”.

Example: Currently, I work as a QA engineer, and I have been in this role since 2022.

Pronoun (B1)

Use 'who' for people in defining relative clauses. Wrong: “This is the colleague which helped me.” → Right: “This is the colleague who helped me.”.

Example: This is the colleague who helped me.

Question (A2)

Use the auxiliary 'does' in present simple questions with 'it'. Wrong: “How long it takes?” → Right: “How long does it take?”.

Example: How long does it take?

Article (A2)

Use an article before a singular countable noun like 'museum'. Wrong: “I want to visit museum this weekend.” → Right: “I want to visit a museum this weekend.”.

Example: I want to visit a museum this weekend.

Preposition (B1)

The standard phrase is 'take care of', not 'take care about'. Wrong: “She takes care about her younger brother.” → Right: “She takes care of her younger brother.”.

Example: She takes care of her younger brother.

Tense (B1)

Use the present continuous for an action happening right now. Wrong: “Right now I work on my master's project.” → Right: “Right now I am working on my master's project.”.

Example: Right now I am working on my master's project.

Verb Pattern (B1)

Use 'would like to' plus the base verb. Wrong: “I would like visit some towns near my city.” → Right: “I would like to visit some towns near my city.”.

Example: I would like to visit some towns near my city.

Countability (B1)

'Vacation' is usually countable in this meaning, so use 'a vacation' for one break. Wrong: “I need some vacation after this month.” → Right: “I need a vacation after this month.”.

Example: I need a vacation after this month.

Word Choice (B1)

'Series' means TV shows. 'Cereal' is food you eat for breakfast. Wrong: “In the evening I like watching films or cereal.” → Right: “In the evening I like watching films or series.”.

Example: In the evening I like watching films or series.

Pronoun (A2)

Use the subject pronoun 'they', not the object pronoun 'them', before the verb. Wrong: “What size are them?” → Right: “What size are they?”.

Example: What size are they?

Preposition (B1)

Use 'full of', not 'full about'. Wrong: “My mind is full about future trips.” → Right: “My mind is full of future trips.”.

Example: My mind is full of future trips.

Tense (B1)

In present simple, add '-s' to the verb after a third-person singular subject like 'this change'. Wrong: “This change affect my whole life.” → Right: “This change affects my whole life.”.

Example: This change affects my whole life.
